bib.title: Neural Codec Language Models are Zero-Shot Text to Speech Synthesizers

question: Can TTS be treated as conditional language modeling over neural audio codec codes, trained on large noisy data, to give zero-shot voice cloning from a 3-second prompt?
hypothesis: Scaling semi-supervised training data to 60K hours and modeling codec tokens with a language model yields GPT-style in-context learning for unseen speakers.
contributions: VALL-E, the first TTS framework with in-context learning, treating TTS as a language-model task over audio codec codes instead of mel spectrograms
A generalized TTS system built on a huge amount of semi-supervised data
Diverse outputs for the same text, keeping the acoustic environment and speaker emotion of the prompt
Better zero-shot results than the state-of-the-art zero-shot TTS system on LibriSpeech and VCTK

method.summary: Text is converted to phonemes and speech to EnCodec codes (8 RVQ quantizers). An autoregressive decoder-only transformer predicts the first-quantizer codes, conditioned on phonemes and the 3-second prompt's first-layer codes. A non-autoregressive transformer predicts quantizers 2 to 8. The EnCodec decoder makes the waveform.

datasets.name: LibriLight
datasets.source: Kahn et al., 2020; audiobooks, audio only
datasets.preprocessing: Transcribed by a hybrid DNN-HMM ASR model trained on 960 hours of LibriSpeech (Kaldi recipe); phoneme alignment with 30ms frameshift; EnCodec codes for all audio; random crop to 10 to 20 s; consecutive phoneme repetitions removed; NAR acoustic prompt is a random 3 s segment of the same utterance

datasets.name: LibriSpeech test-clean
datasets.size: 2.2 hours subset (utterances 4 to 10 s); 40 speakers for human evaluation
datasets.preprocessing: enrolled speech is a 3 s crop of another utterance of the same speaker

datasets.name: VCTK
datasets.preprocessing: three utterances per speaker as 3s/5s/10s prompts, text from another utterance

datasets.name: EmoV-DB
datasets.preprocessing: prompts for qualitative emotion test only

models.name: VALL-E AR model
models.architecture: decoder-only causal transformer over first-quantizer codes
models.tokenizer: EnCodec 24 kHz, 75 Hz, 8 quantizers x 1024 entries (6K bitrate); phonemes via G2P

models.name: VALL-E NAR model
models.architecture: same transformer as AR, full attention, eight separate acoustic embeddings, stage injected by AdaLN

other.note: open-sourced code run with released model
WER copied from its paper; not open-source

training.objective: maximise p(C | x, C~): next-token prediction of first-codebook codes (AR); NAR trained on a randomly sampled stage i in [2,8]
training.seq_len: random crop of 10 to 20 s of audio (average utterance 60 s)

other.AR_prompting_in_training: no explicit prompt clip; any prefix acts as prompt
other.weight_sharing: output projection shared with acoustic embedding

inference.decoding: AR: sampling-based (beam search can loop forever); NAR: greedy
inference.samples: LibriSpeech: each experiment run three times, average reported; diversity figure uses two runs with different seeds
inference.prompting: Prepend the enrolled speech's transcript phonemes to the target phonemes; the enrolled speech's first-layer codes are the AR prefix; all eight layers of the prompt are summed for NAR. VALL-E-continual uses the first 3 s of the utterance and its full transcript.

metrics.name: WER
metrics.definition: HuBERT-Large fine-tuned on LibriSpeech 960h (CTC, no LM) transcribes the output; WER against original transcript

metrics.name: SPK
metrics.definition: WavLM-TDNN speaker-verification similarity between prompt (decompressed enrolled speech) and synthesis, range [-1, 1]

metrics.name: SMOS
metrics.definition: similarity MOS, 1 to 5 in 0.5 steps, 6 native-speaker raters

metrics.name: CMOS
metrics.definition: comparative MOS for naturalness, -3 to 3 in steps of 1, 12 native-speaker raters

eval.protocol: Crowdsourced human evaluation; LibriSpeech 40 test cases, VCTK 60 speakers (11 unseen to YourTTS, 49 seen). No significance test described beyond +/- values.

availability.code: https://github.com/microsoft/unilm (listed on title page; demo at aka.ms/valle)
availability.data: LibriLight, LibriSpeech, VCTK are public; generated transcripts not stated as released

evidence.quote: The models are trained using 16 NVIDIA TESLA V100 32GB GPUs with a batch size of 6k acoustic tokens per GPU for 800k steps.

limits: Synthesis robustness: words may be unclear, missed or duplicated because the AR stage has unconstrained attention alignment.
Data coverage: 60K hours does not cover accented speakers; worse VCTK than LibriSpeech similarity; LibriLight is read-style audiobooks only.
Two separate models (AR and NAR) for the quantizers; authors suggest a single universal model or fully NAR.
Misuse risk: spoofing voice identification or impersonation; mitigation suggested is a detection model, not built.
Comparison with YourTTS on VCTK is unfair because YourTTS trained on 97 of its speakers; GSLM/AudioLM comparison mixes different ASR for AudioLM; AudioLM speaker score not computed.
Weights not stated as released; no parameter count, precision, seeds, temperature or top-p given; evaluation raters are small (12 and 6) with no significance test described.

terms.definition: the whole transcription and the first 3 seconds of the utterance are the phoneme and acoustic prompts, and the model generates the continuation

lineage.note: follows it in using neural codec tokens; VALL-E is TTS rather than speech-to-speech

figures.caption: The overview of VALL-E. Unlike the previous pipeline (e.g., phoneme -> mel-spectrogram -> waveform), the pipeline of VALL-E is phoneme -> discrete code -> waveform.

figures.caption: The structure of the conditional codec language modeling, which is built in a hierarchical manner.
